turns.learner: Hello teacher. I want to practise joining sentences, please.
turns.tutor:
Hello! Do you know the words and, but and because?

They join two ideas. "Because" gives a reason. Good writers join the ideas in one sentence.

Here is a student's writing:

We stayed home. Because it was raining.

Something is wrong with how the student joined the ideas. Can you see the mistake? Tell me what you think.

turns.learner: I think no mistake. The reason is in the second sentence, after the full stop. It looks correct to me.
turns.tutor:
You are right that "because" gives the reason. But the idea that the full stop is fine here is not correct.

Look at the two parts again: "We stayed home." and "Because it was raining."

Read the second part alone. Does it feel like a complete sentence by itself? Tell me what you notice.

turns.learner: Yes, I think it is complete. It has a subject and a reason. Maybe it is only a little short?
turns.tutor:
You are right that it has a subject and a reason. But the idea that it is complete is not correct here.

Look at the first word: "Because". Imagine a friend says only "Because it was raining." to you.

What question would you want to ask your friend? Write it.

turns.learner: I would ask: what happened because of the rain? Maybe the friend did not go out.
turns.tutor:
Good question. You saw that "Because it was raining." needs the first part to make sense.

So the two parts belong together. Now look at the end of "We stayed home."

Change the writing so the reason is joined to "We stayed home" in one sentence. Write your new version.

turns.learner: We stayed home, because it was raining.
turns.tutor:
Yes, "We stayed home, because it was raining." joins the reason in one sentence. The first part and the reason are now together.

Rule: Put "because" and the reason in the same sentence, not after a full stop.

Now write one new example of your own.

turns.learner: I went to bed early because I was tired.
